questions.question: For a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, what is a minimum spanning tree?
options: The set of the shortest edges, one chosen at each vertex of the network
A tree of shortest paths from one origin vertex to all other vertices
A spanning tree with the smallest total edge length of all spanning trees
A spanning tree that uses as few edges as possible to reach all vertices

questions.question: A planner has a network of towns and possible connections with nonnegative lengths. Which planning question is answered by a minimum spanning tree of this network?
options: Which route from the depot to each town has the least travel length?
Which closed route travels every connection exactly once in total?
In which order should a single vehicle visit all towns, returning home?
Which connections link all towns with the least total length built?

questions.question: Two analysts find different minimum spanning trees of the same connected network with nonnegative edge lengths. What must hold?
options: One of them must have made a calculation error.
Their total lengths may differ by a tie amount.
Both trees must share every edge of equal length.
Both trees have exactly the same total length.

questions.question: A network of towns with nonnegative road lengths falls into two groups, with no road between the groups. What can be said about a minimum spanning tree of this network?
options: None exists, since no spanning tree links the groups.
It is formed by a cheapest tree within each group.
It exists after adding a zero-length road between them.
It is the cheapest tree in the larger of the two groups.

questions.question: A student claims that in a connected network with $n$ vertices and nonnegative lengths, the $n-1$ shortest edges always form a minimum spanning tree. Which network refutes this claim?
options: Path $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$ with lengths 1, 2 and 3, and no other edges
Triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ with lengths 1, 2 and 3, and no other edges
Square $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$–$A$ with lengths 1, 1, 1 and 5 in this order
Triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ with all lengths 1, plus edge $C$–$D$ of length 5

questions.question: A network is the triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ with lengths 4 on $A$–$B$, 6 on $B$–$C$ and 5 on $A$–$C$. What is the total length of its minimum spanning tree?
A network is the cycle $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$–$A$ with lengths 3 on $A$–$B$, 5 on $B$–$C$, 2 on $C$–$D$ and 7 on $D$–$A$. What is the total length of its minimum spanning tree?

A network is the triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ with lengths 5 on $A$–$B$, 4 on $B$–$C$ and 6 on $A$–$C$. Its minimum spanning tree is used as a road network. How long is the trip from $A$ to $C$ along this tree?
options: 6, along $A$–$C$
15, all three
4, along $B$–$C$
9, through $B$

questions.question: A spanning tree $T$ has edges $A$–$B$ (6), $B$–$C$ (2) and $C$–$D$ (3), total 11. The network also has the edge $A$–$C$ of length 4. Adding $A$–$C$ to $T$ and dropping one edge of the cycle formed gives a cheaper spanning tree. What is its total length?
options: 13, dropping $B$–$C$
9, dropping $A$–$B$
10, dropping $C$–$D$
11, dropping $A$–$C$

questions.question: In a network on 6 vertices every pair of vertices is joined by an edge, and all 15 edges have length 3. What is the total length of a minimum spanning tree, and which spanning trees attain it?
options: 18, as six edges of length 3 are needed
15, but only one tree attains it
15, and every spanning tree attains it
45, the total length of all 15 edges

questions.question: In a connected network with $n$ vertices and nonnegative lengths, the same positive constant $c$ is added to every edge length. What happens to the minimum spanning trees?
options: They can change, since short edges gain relatively more.
They stay the same only if $c$ is smaller than every length.
They stay the same; each tree's total rises by $(n-1)c$.
They stay the same, and the minimum total is unchanged.

questions.question: In a connected network with nonnegative lengths, an edge $e$ lies on a cycle and is strictly longer than every other edge of that cycle. Can $e$ belong to a minimum spanning tree?
options: Yes: a tree must contain at least one edge of every cycle.
No: swapping it for another cycle edge gives a shorter tree.
Only if every other edge of the cycle is also in the tree.
Only when $e$ is also the longest edge of the network.

questions.question: In a connected network with nonnegative lengths, the edge $f$ is strictly shorter than every other edge. Which minimum spanning trees contain $f$?
options: Only some of them, depending on the other lengths.
None of them need it, since one short edge saves little.
All of them: any tree without $f$ can be shortened.
Only those in which an endpoint of $f$ is a leaf.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ (4), $A$–$C$ (1), $B$–$C$ (3), $B$–$D$ (2) and $C$–$D$ (5). Comparing all its spanning trees, what is the total length of a minimum spanning tree?
A network is the cycle $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$–$A$ with lengths 1 on $A$–$B$, 4 on $B$–$C$, 2 on $C$–$D$ and 4 on $D$–$A$. How many minimum spanning trees does it have, and what is their total length?
options: Two, each of total length 7
One, of total length 7
Four, each of total length 7
Two, of total lengths 7 and 10

questions.question: A network has the triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ with lengths 1, 2, 3 on $A$–$B$, $B$–$C$, $C$–$A$, the triangle $D$–$E$–$F$ with lengths 1, 1, 4 on $D$–$E$, $E$–$F$, $F$–$D$, and one edge $C$–$D$ of length 20. What is the total length of a minimum spanning tree?
In a connected network with nonnegative lengths, how does the presence of two edges with equal length relate to having more than one minimum spanning tree?
options: Two equal lengths always produce at least two minimum trees.
Ties are needed for several minimum trees but do not guarantee them.
Equal lengths are needed for, and also produce, several minimum trees.
Several minimum trees can arise even when all lengths are different.

questions.question: The definition of a minimum spanning tree assumes nonnegative edge lengths. If the goal is the cheapest set of edges that connects all vertices, why does this assumption matter?
options: With nonnegative lengths every spanning tree has $n-1$ edges, which fails for negative lengths.
With nonnegative lengths dropping a cycle edge never adds cost, so a cheapest connection is a tree.
With nonnegative lengths the cheapest connection also gives the shortest travel routes between vertices.
With nonnegative lengths every spanning tree has the same total, so the choice is easy.

questions.question: A network is the cycle $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$–$A$ with lengths 2 on $A$–$B$, 3 on $B$–$C$, 4 on $C$–$D$ and 6 on $D$–$A$, so $A$–$B$, $B$–$C$, $C$–$D$ form a minimum spanning tree. Up to which length can $C$–$D$ be increased while this tree remains a minimum spanning tree?
options: Up to 6, the length of $D$–$A$
Up to 4, its current length
Up to 5, one unit more than 4
Up to any length, since it is in the tree

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ (1), $B$–$C$ (2), $C$–$D$ (3), $A$–$D$ (4) and $A$–$C$ (5). The planner insists that the link $A$–$C$ is built. What is the smallest total length of a spanning tree that contains $A$–$C$?
